title: ALONGate
text:
The border region between Iceland, Norway and Greenland forms a central biogeographical corridor through which fauna adapted to extreme environmental conditions spread to the Arctic Ocean via the North Atlantic Gate. Although extensive biodiversity data are available for this region, analyses reveal significant gaps between frequently sampled areas, particularly in deep and remote zones.
ALONGate addresses these gaps by investigating biodiversity along spatial and temporal gradients and by linking data from established programmes around Iceland, including BIOICE (Benthic Invertebrates of Icelandic Waters, 1992–2004) and IceAGE (Icelandic Marine Animals: Genetics and Ecology, since 2011), with new observations towards the Arctic.
Since 2023, annual sampling with the epibenthic sled (EBS) in the HAUSGARTEN area of the Alfred Wegener Institute has provided fundamental insights into the local distribution of warm- and cold-water species. In addition, samples taken along a north-south transect from Iceland to the Fram Strait are closing important knowledge gaps to better understand future shifts in faunal communities in the north.
In-situ sampling along latitudinal and longitudinal deep-sea transects is complemented by the deployment of Benthic Lander Observatory Systems (BLOS) at critical junctions. Particular focus is placed on capturing images and videos of sensitive marine ecosystems (VMEs), such as hydrothermal vents and cold-water coral reefs (CWC), over seasonal cycles.
Based on an integrated dataset of abiotic parameters (bathymetry, benthic oxygen uptake, sediment samples) and biotic data (macrofauna samples, imagery), a comprehensive comparison of macro- and megafauna communities is created. This contributes significantly to a deeper understanding of benthic biodiversity and its controlling environmental factors.

title: ALONGate
text:
The current technological development allows to observe annual cycles via stationary observatories. In total, four ALONGate benthic lander observatory systems (BLOS) are built in 2024-2025 in the Senckenberg workshop Wilhelmshaven in cooperation with the Alfred Wegener Institute (AWI) and IFREMER.
Currently, the first BLOS is tested at the Senckenberg workshop and a second system will be delivered via IFREMER partners in October 2024. By mid-25 all planned BLOS should be available and can be prepared for deployment. The present shiptime application is the “kick off expedition” for regular deployments of the BLOS.
The plan is a regular redeployment (every second year) throughout ALONGate’s lifetime. While we cannot reach comprehensive sampling or predictions in the comparably unexplored regions of the deep sea within five years, ALONGate uses the comparably well-studied area around Iceland as natural experimental and a key area to find the balance between protection and sustainable use of the ocean (for example by fisheries).
The BLOS will collect image and video data at regular intervals along with abiotic data (temperature, salinity, and other CTD measures) and optionally could be equipped with further sensors supplied by cooperation partners. A maximum of 16 sensors can be plugged in to the battery system.
The technical design has already been tested with equipment deployed at “Lucky Strike” (EMSO Azores, Metabos et al. 2022) and the “Aurora” vent field (Ramirez-Llodra et a. 2023). During this shiptime application for 2026 and 2027 we propose eight different working areas (WA1 – WA8) representing different habitats and Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems (VMEs): cold-water-corals reefs (WA1&2: Skeiðarárdjúp fishery closure and Lóndsjúp trough), sponge gardens and closed fishing grounds neighboring direct fishing impacted areas North of Iceland (WA3), WAs 4 to 6 complementing the deep-sea transect complementary to the Hausgarten longitudinal transect in the Fram Strait (but at the Southern end of the North Atlantic Gateway area) and the BLOS deployment in 2025 during ALONGate1 with RV Polarstern, hydrothermal vents (WA7: Grímsey) and as well as the highly fishery impacted area Dohrn bank off Greenland in the Denmark Strait (WA8). At three areas (WA1, 2 and 7), either restoration experiments or benthic observatory lander systems (BLOS) will be deployed. At WA6 a deep-sea lander from AWI will be deployed like planned for the secondary use of RV Polarstern in 2025/2026. All eight WAs are included in the application for 2026, but only BLOS and deep-sea lander recovery sites are included in the calculation of 2027 (WAs 1, 2, 6 and 7). In the following, we outline the status quo of research reflecting the knowledge related to our proposed WAs. The focus on four BLOS is necessary because the chosen deployment sites need to ensure that the deployed BLOS are not endangered by fishery impact and lost due to fishing activities. Thus, the BLOS can only be deployed at fishery closures (see Table 1 & 2) or at deep stations below the depth of fishing activity. The deep-sea East-West transect complements the deep-sea lander deployments and filling the transect with standardized sampling is the second focus of the present shiptime application. Because of the baseline character of the deep-sea transects, the transect is only planned in year 2026, while in 2027 the shiptime is designated for BLOS recovery and re-sampling of the BLOS WAs as new LTER sites.

title: New and Old Isopods
text:
A new isopod species was discovered at the Nidhogg chimney (3016 m) in the Jøtul vent field and the deep-sea Amundsen Basin (4156 m) in the Artic Ocean. Based on the morphological and molecular evidence, a new genus will be erected including the previously described Jaera tyleri Malyutina & Brandt, 2014. Both species from the newly erected genus share a set of traits, that significantly differ from the rest of the typically shallow-water Jaera species. Two of such characters stood out: they were both sampled at abyssal depth, and presumably both feed on bacteria. While J. tyleri was collected on whale bones and grazing on the bacterial community on the bones, the new species were found at an active hydrothermal vent site and presumably feeds on the chemosynthetic bacteria.



CLSM scans of the new isopod species in dorsal and ventral views (Kohlenbach et al., under review)


The necessity of a taxonomic revision of Jaera Leach, 1814 has already been recognized, as well as the enclosing family Janiridae G.O. Sars, 1897, which is proven to be polyphyletic. This study contributes the first step in resolving the systematics of these groups and our understanding to the ecology of isopods inhabiting chemosynthetic environments.



Stations of the sampling campaign, red points indicates the locations where the new species was found (Kohlenbach et al., under review)

title: New and Old Isopods
text:
Disconectes coxalis Kussakin, 1983
Disconectes coxalis was officially described by Kussakin in 1983, but the type materials was lost later. Adding to the only four individuals collected from Canadian Basins from 3100 to 3400 m depth, approx. 70 specimens of this species were collected at the Eurasian part of the Arctic Ocean during the ArcWatch-1 expedition onboard RV Polarstern, exactly 40 years after the species was described. The newly collected specimens will be used for the re-description along with molecular data.
Although being sampled in the central Arctic Ocean, this species has not been found elsewhere, particularly at the Hausgarten LTER in the Fram Strait, which represents the only deep channel connecting Arctic Ocean with other Ocean sectors. Based on this, D. coxalis are suggested to be endemic in the Arctic.
